passage: Tutor's note, Thursday. Yamini's classmates did an imitation of her accent in the corridor today, and one of them, Vaibhav, held his nose at her home-cooked lunch and said, "just banter, yaar." Yamini laughed along, but her eyes went to the floor and she wrapped her tiffin in her bag quickly. At the end of the day I asked her to stay back. She said, "I laugh so they don't think I'm sensitive. But it hurts." I told her the mockery was not hers to carry. She practised a plain sentence with me: "That's not okay with me." Yamini said it to Vaibhav on Friday morning, and he went quiet, then said sorry. I have spoken to the whole class about mimicry. I will check in with her next week.

qa.q: What did Vaibhav do at Yamini's lunch?
qa.a: Vaibhav held his nose at her home-cooked lunch and called it just banter.

qa.q: Why did Yamini laugh along with the mimicking?
qa.a: She laughed so people would not think she was sensitive, though it hurt her.

qa.q: What plain sentence helped Yamini respond?
qa.a: She practised the sentence "That's not okay with me" and said it to Vaibhav.

qa.q: How might Vaibhav have seen the mimicry before Yamini spoke up?
qa.a: As harmless banter, since Yamini laughed along, though her reply made him go quiet and apologise.

grounding: Classmates mimic her accent and food and call it banter; she laughs along while hurt, then tells them plainly it is not fine.

passage:
Gargi, you want the honest version for your podcast? Okay. I'm Farhan, from Srinagar, and first year in Delhi my hostel floor made my accent their favourite joke. Every time I said anything, someone would repeat it in a long, drawn-out voice. They called my mother's kahwa "grass water". They said it was banter.

And I laughed. Every time. I thought laughing meant I was one of them. But I stopped talking in the mess. I stopped bringing kahwa.

One evening, someone did the voice when I was asking for the salt, and I just said, "Stop. I don't find it funny. It's how I talk." Silence. Then one guy said, "Sorry, man." Two others kept at it for a while and I stopped sitting with them.

Now my closest friends are the ones who asked me to teach them how to make kahwa.

qa.q: What did the hostel floor call Farhan's mother's kahwa?
How did Farhan feel while laughing along with the jokes?
qa.a: Farhan felt hurt and lonely, pretending to belong while quietly withdrawing from the mess and hiding the kahwa.

qa.q: What did Farhan do that changed things?
qa.a: Farhan told them plainly to stop and then chose to spend time with people who respected that accent and food.

qa.q: How might the guy who said "Sorry, man" have seen the jokes before that evening?
qa.a: That classmate may have thought it was harmless fun because Farhan always laughed, and only saw the hurt when Farhan spoke up.

grounding: The monologue shows a young person whose accent and food are mocked as banter, who stops laughing along, speaks up and finds people who respect those roots.

passage:
First week. At the Chennai college canteen, Jasleen opened her tiffin and the table erupted. "Ooh, Punjabi aunty ka paratha! Where's the butter tanker?" Someone did a loud, fake accent. Jasleen laughed hardest of all. Inside, her face was hot.

Fourth week. She stopped bringing parathas. She bought idlis from the canteen and practised flattening her accent in the mirror. Mum asked on the phone why she sounded tired.

Seventh week, a Monday. Nitin put on the accent again at the library steps. Jasleen's stomach twisted. This time she said, "Nitin, that's not fine. I've laughed because I didn't want to be the odd one out. It hurts."

Nitin blinked. "I didn't... okay. Sorry."

That Friday she brought parathas again, and a girl from her lab asked for the recipe.

qa.q: What did Jasleen buy from the canteen in the fourth week?
qa.a: She bought idlis from the canteen.

qa.q: What was Jasleen feeling when she laughed hardest of all in the first week?
qa.a: Jasleen felt embarrassed and hurt, hot-faced inside while pretending to find it funny.

qa.q: What went wrong in the fourth week, and what fixed it?
qa.a: Jasleen hid her food and accent to fit in; telling Nitin plainly that the joke hurt and bringing parathas again fixed it.

qa.q: How might Nitin have seen the joke before Jasleen spoke up?
qa.a: Nitin probably thought it was harmless because Jasleen laughed, and was surprised to learn it hurt.

grounding: The three beats show a young woman mocked for her accent and food who first hides her roots, then tells a classmate plainly it is not fine.
